items.prompt: An HR administrator tries to approve their own pending leave request. What happens?
items.answer: 403, as no one may decide their own request, not even HR
distractors: 200, as HR may approve any request, their own included
409, as it must first be reassigned to another HR admin
200, but the decision is flagged for a later audit review
items.explanation: decide rejects current.employee.userId === actor.id with 'You cannot approve or reject your own leave request.' before checking HR or direct-manager authority.

items.prompt: A MANAGER who is not the employee's current direct manager tries to approve that employee's leave. What does decide check, and what happens?
items.answer: 404, as the scoped lookup reaches only the manager's current reports
distractors: 200, as any user holding the MANAGER role may decide any employee's leave
200, as decide trusts the managerId that the request body supplies
200, as decide trusts the manager id baked into the JWT at login
items.explanation: decide first loads the request through scoped(), which filters by employeeScope: for a MANAGER that is their own profile or employees whose manager is them, read from the database now, so another manager's report's request is 'not found within your access' (404); the later direct-manager 403 check is defence in depth, and the body carries only intent (version, status, note).

items.prompt: A manager approved a request (now version 2). HR then sends a REJECTED decision carrying version 2. Why is it still refused?
items.answer: It is refused because the request is no longer PENDING
distractors: It succeeds because the version matches the current record
It is refused because only the original manager may change it
It is refused because version 2 is for approvals
items.explanation: Each guard protects a different invariant: the version check catches stale drafts; the PENDING check (and status in the updateMany where) blocks re-deciding a terminal request.

items.prompt: An employee has approved leave July 10-12. Which new request is rejected as overlapping?
distractors: July 13-15
July 13-14
July 7-9
items.explanation: The exclusion constraint uses daterange(startDate, endDate, '[]') with &&, for PENDING or APPROVED rows.

items.prompt: Overlap is checked by the repository under an employee row lock AND by a PostgreSQL exclusion constraint. What does each layer contribute?
items.answer: The app check gives a clear error, the constraint stops bypassing writes
distractors: They are redundant, and the constraint exists only for performance
The app check covers approved leave, the constraint pending leave
The constraint gives the clear error, and the app check is a SQLite fallback
items.explanation: Commenting out the constraint fails the test that inserts directly with Prisma, while the concurrent-HTTP test still passes because of the row lock.

items.prompt: You remove status: 'PENDING' from decide's updateMany where clause and the whole suite stays green. What should you conclude?
items.answer: The guards overlap, so find the smallest set whose removal a test notices
distractors: The status filter is dead code and should be deleted from decide
The tests are broken and should be rewritten until this change fails
PostgreSQL enforces the PENDING rule by itself through a constraint
items.explanation: Removing the pre-check as well makes HR's version-2 rejection return 200 and overwrite the approval; removing one of several overlapping guards proves nothing.

items.prompt: chartLock takes pg_advisory_xact_lock(74219801), one constant key. What does that guarantee and what does it cost?
items.answer: Edits cannot jointly form a cycle, but every employee write serializes
distractors: It locks only the employee being edited, so unrelated edits run in parallel
It prevents leave overlaps across the organization, slowing directory reads
It rules out deadlocks anywhere, at the cost of extra memory
items.explanation: The simple, provably correct option pays in throughput; a per-chain key is finer but must lock both roots in a fixed order when a change joins two chains.

items.prompt: With the constant chart lock in place, how do leave-request writes behave?
items.answer: They skip the advisory lock but queue on the same employee's row lock
distractors: They also wait on the chart lock, so every leave write is serialized too
They take no locks and rely on the exclusion constraint alone
They lock the whole Employee table for the length of the transaction
items.explanation: Leave writes call lockEmployee (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on one Employee row), not chartLock.

items.prompt: Two HR administrators deactivate each other at the same time. Why does 'keep at least one active HR administrator' hold today, and what would break it?
items.answer: chartLock serializes the count-then-update, which a per-chain lock breaks
distractors: A unique partial index on active HR admins enforces it inside PostgreSQL
It does not hold, and both deactivations succeed today with no HR admin left
The frontend hides the deactivate button for the last HR administrator
items.explanation: Before narrowing a lock, list everything it serializes, not only the reason it was added.

items.prompt: A plain EMPLOYEE calls GET /api/employees/options directly. What do they get?
items.answer: The id and name of every active manager and HR administrator
distractors: A 403, as the route uses requireHr like every employee mutation
Their own profile alone, as employeeScope limits the options query
An empty list, as the options are filtered by the caller's department
items.explanation: Scope is enforced on the main list but forgotten on a helper list, the pattern to look for in every review; no integration test touches the route.

items.prompt: In the bounded manager filter design, a manager filters by another manager's id. Why return an empty result rather than 403?
items.answer: The filter intersects with employeeScope, and a 403 would leak the id exists
distractors: A 403 response cannot be cached by React Query, so the list would flicker
Managers are allowed to see other managers' direct reports anyway
Validation runs after the query, so the 403 would come too late
items.explanation: For HR the scope is {}, so the filter is a real filter; for others it safely intersects rather than rejects.

items.prompt: A manager loses a direct report to another team. What happens when they open that report's old leave history?
items.answer: An empty list, as history follows the caller's current scope
distractors: Their full history, as they decided those requests at the time
A 404, as the requests moved with the employee to the new manager
The full history, as audit rows are public within a department
items.explanation: Returning [] hides whether the request exists and keeps working after deletion, but using current scope means history access follows today's reporting line.

items.front: Why must a draft loaded at version 1 send expected version 1 even if another tab saved version 2?
items.back: The version records the state the user actually reviewed. Attaching the latest version to an old draft would bypass conflict detection; conditional writes include the baseline version and the UI keeps the rejected input for export and reconciliation.

items.front: Why does decide read the leave request, lock the employee row, then read it again?
items.back: The first scoped read authorizes and finds which employee to lock; the second is needed because a competing operation may have completed while the lock was being acquired. Decide only on the post-lock read.

items.front: useEffect(() => setPage(1), [query, active]) resets pagination after a filter change. What is wrong?
items.back: It runs one render late: for one render the query key pairs the new filter with the old page, so React Query fetches e.g. page 3 of the filtered list first. Reset the page in the same event handler that changes the filter.

items.front: How do you test an approval race properly?
items.back: Send two decisions with the same saved version (approve and reject). Expect exactly one success and one 409, then read the row and audit: version advanced once, the recorded decider is the winner, the losing note did not overwrite. Asserting 'no 500' alone misses the bug.
